extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly — educated public, authors, critics, and policymakers interested in science, literature, and public affairs
extracted.subtask_description: Magazine editorials and literary notices evaluating books, reviews, public reports, and debates between science and theology; provides guidance on fair reviewing, topical surveys, and public-interest publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address moral concepts when discussing property/possession
rubrics_metrics.description: When treating transactions involving 'possession,' 'appropriation of property,' 'robbery,' 'criminality,' 'penalty,' etc., one should also consider 'justice,' 'equity,' 'duty,' 'right,' and 'wrong,' and principles of obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page criticizes authors who omit moral elements of inquiries about property and possession as engaging in 'wordy circuits' to avoid fundamentals; discussions of rights (e.g., to life or to property) should consider whether natural rights exist and how law should be shaped to give effect to such principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge author's natural claim to their production
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors seek the pleasure and profit of having at their disposal what they produce and claim to be allowed to turn it to account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues against treating literary production as having no natural right of property and criticizes the view that ownership depends solely on political vote ('If the ayes have it, he has; if the noes have it, he has not'). Reviewers and commentators should recognize the author's stake in their productions beyond mere legislative grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review works in proper context with reference to previous volumes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a book is part of a series, critics should reference previous volumes and indicate how the current work fits in; without that context a critical understanding is incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Times' review is faulted for reviewing a Spencer volume without referring to earlier works in the series; reviewers should avoid taking a work out of its series-context and thereby making it appear deficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid silence; give fair attention to influential works
rubrics_metrics.description: Influential works that are molding opinion and guiding thought should not be ignored by leading journals and reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page condemns journals that adopt a policy of silence (ignoring an author's works) and implies that fair critical practice requires acknowledging and engaging with widely read and influential writings rather than systematic neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misrepresentation; practice decency and fairness in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics should not assail works with 'reckless misrepresentations' and should maintain decency and fairness rather than being influenced by publishers or other agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recounts that Spencer's works were 'assailed with such reckless misrepresentations' that he ceased sending copies to the press; guidance: be accurate, impartial, and resist being bribed, placated, or flattered—criticism should be honest and fair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rashly accuse physical science of atheism; distinguish methodological scope
rubrics_metrics.description: It is undesirable to throw about the reproach of atheism rashly; physical science, properly so called, is compelled by its nature to take no account of the being of God (methodological neutrality) and therefore is 'atheous' (without recognition) but not necessarily atheistic (denying God).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Bishop of Carlisle's position is cited: theologians should distinguish the scientific attitude (working from observed facts and conclusions drawn from them, i.e., 'atheous') from an atheistic state of mind; accusing science of being atheistic is a mistaken policy—examine the method and limits of scientific investigation before levelling such charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey books should present salient features with judicious materials and proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: A survey of a large subject should present its salient features, use materials judiciously, and treat subjects in approximately their relative proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice of Escott's survey praises 'a judicious use of materials' and balanced treatment across topics (village life, landholders, law-courts, working-classes, education, intellectual life). Evaluate such books on readability, coverage balance, and the quality of contributors (e.g., notable chapters by recognized authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-interest books should disclose authorship; anonymity invites suspicion
rubrics_metrics.description: In treating a great public interest openly and candidly there should be no occasion for the concealment of authorship; anonymous publication in such contexts is questionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Interoceanic Canal pamphlet is criticized for anonymity—if an author has a rival interest he might withhold his name, but for public matters authorship disclosure is the norm; lack of transparency suggests possible ulterior motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy/pamphlet critiques should identify bias and avoid narrow nationalistic advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Works aimed at public policy should be judged for spirit and fairness; narrow, bigoted, or illiberal national policies are to be criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Interoceanic Canal book is described as 'narrow in spirit' and 'advocates a bigoted and illiberal national policy'—assess pamphlets for breadth, objectivity, and whether they employ the Monroe Doctrine or other pretexts to advance partisan aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate arguments about machinery's impact on labor with empirical multi-factor evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about machinery should be examined for evidence on (1) effects on cost of food and goods, (2) demand for labor and employment levels, (3) length of the working-day and muscular exertion required, and (4) confounding factors (e.g., immigration) that affect outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The summary of Powers' essay lists four empirical conclusions (reduced cost of necessities; increased demand for labor; reduced working-day and exertion; immigration as a confounder). When assessing such claims, require quantitative data and consider population movements and other external factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public works reports should include full condition statements, surveys, estimates, and early-action recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: A municipal public-works report should give a very full and elaborate statement of the condition of infrastructure (e.g., water-supply), surveys of potential sources, storage capacities, drainage areas, estimated costs, projected supply vs demand, and urge early action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New York Department of Public Works report is commended for detailed surveys (Bronx, Byram, Housatonic), storage capacity estimates, daily supply projections, and cost estimates; evaluators should look for such comprehensive data and explicit recommendations to commence timely works to meet increasing demand.
